bibl.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the contribution of each individual input pixel to one non-linear classifier's decision on one image
span.quote: The overall idea of pixel-wise decomposition is to understand the contribution of a single pixel of an image x to the prediction f(x) made by a classifier f in an image classification task. We would like to find out, separately for each image x, which pixels contribute to what extent to a positive or negative classification result.

span.label: how to explain why a non-linear image classifier reached a particular decision, at the resolution of single pixels
span.quote: However, like many methods in machine learning, these models often lack a straightforward interpretability of the classifier predictions. In other words the classifier acts as a black box and does not provide detailed information about why it reaches a certain classification decision.

span.label: layer-wise relevance propagation - a heatmapping concept defined as a set of constraints rather than an algorithm - together with a Taylor-type alternative, both applicable to pre-trained Bag-of-Words and neural classifiers
span.quote: We will introduce layer-wise relevance propagation as a concept defined by a set of constraints. Any solution satisfying the constraints will be considered to follow the concept of layer-wise relevance propagation.

span.label: method
span.quote: The overall idea of pixel-wise decomposition is to understand the contribution of a single pixel of an image x to the prediction f(x) made by a classifier f in an image classification task. We would like to find out, separately for each image x, which pixels contribute to what extent to a positive or negative classification result.

span.label: classifier opacity: a non-linear model gives a decision without saying what in the input produced it
span.quote: However, like many methods in machine learning, these models often lack a straightforward interpretability of the classifier predictions. In other words the classifier acts as a black box and does not provide detailed information about why it reaches a certain classification decision.

span.label: redistribute the prediction backwards layer by layer under a conservation constraint until it rests on the input pixels
span.term: redistribute the prediction backwards layer by layer under a conservation constraint until it rests on the input pixels
span.quote: The underlying Formula (2) can be interpreted as a conservation law for the relevance R in between layers of the feature processing.

span.label: the relevance held by a unit is redistributed onto the units that fed it, and the total is preserved from one layer to the next, so the prediction survives intact all the way down to the pixels
span.quote: The underlying Formula (2) can be interpreted as a conservation law for the relevance R in between layers of the feature processing.

span.label: relevance is computed one layer at a time rather than globally, which is cheap but can strand relevance in a lower layer where it is then distributed randomly
span.quote: A first aspect that needs to be investigated is the greediness of the layer-wise relevance propagation procedure, in the sense that it is computed one layer at a time, and its potential impact on the quality of heatmaps: While computationally advantageous, some of the backpropagated relevance might encounter a dead-end in the lower layers and be distributed randomly.

span.label: the gradient at the prediction point points toward the nearest local optimum, which may carry the SAME SIGN as the prediction - so it does not point at the boundary the explanation is relative to
span.quote: The differential Df(x) at the prediction point does not necessarily point to a root which is close under the Euclidean norm.

span.label: a root is found by taking any candidate with the opposite prediction sign and searching the line between them - the segment must cross zero, so interval intersection locates it
span.quote: It is clear that the line l(a) = ax + (1 − a)x′ must contain a root of f which can be found by interval intersection.

span.label: the root point is specified by CONSTRAINTS rather than by a formula - it must be a root and must lie near the data point, with the rest deferred
span.quote: In particular, the root point x 0 at which the Taylor decomposition is computed is constrained to satisfy f(x 0) = 0 and to lie not too far (e.g. within a fixed radius) from the actual data point x.

span.label: the two approaches differ in what they conserve: the earlier work rectifies activations to keep feature maps non-negative, this one uses SIGNED activations to conserve the relevance quantity across layers
span.quote: uses rectified linear units to project information from the unfolded maps towards the inputs with the aim to ensure the feature maps to be non-negative.

span.label: the propagation is greedy - computed one layer at a time - and some relevance may hit a dead end in the lower layers and be distributed randomly
span.quote: A first aspect that needs to be investigated is the greediness of the layer-wise relevance propagation procedure, in the sense that it is computed one layer at a time, and its potential impact on the quality of heatmaps: While computationally advantageous, some of the backpropagated relevance might encounter a dead-end in the lower layers and be distributed randomly.

span.label: the proposed propagation rules are heuristic: whether relevance proportional to weighted neuron activations can be analytically justified is open
span.quote: Another open question relates to the heuristic nature of the proposed instances of relevance propagation, in particular, whether the distributed relevance messages being proportional to the weighted neuron activations can be analytically justified.

span.label: there is no way to evaluate the quality of a heatmap beyond looking at it
span.quote: Finally, it is not clear how to evaluate the quality of a heatmap beyond simple visual assessment.

span.label: no universal metric for quantifying heatmap quality exists; the paper defers it to future work
span.quote: Future work will need to explore the many domain- and data-specific degrees of freedom in the heatmapping process in order to ultimately propose a universal metric for quantification.

span.label: a decomposition satisfying the conservation equation is neither unique nor guaranteed to be meaningful - the constraint set does not pin down an answer
span.quote: As we will show now, a decomposition satisfying Eq (2) per se is neither unique, nor it is guaranteed that it yields a meaningful interpretation of the classifier prediction.

span.label: the Taylor approach needs a second point besides the input, and finding it is called a technical difficulty in the paper's own words
span.quote: One technical difficulty is to find a root point x 0.

span.label: where several minimal-norm roots exist the method must average or integrate over them rather than pick one
span.quote: In case of multiple existing roots x 0 with minimal norm, they can be averaged or integrated in order to get an average over all these solutions.

span.label: a competing method is specific to convolutional architectures, which the paper contrasts with its own range of applicability
span.quote: This work is specific to the architecture of convolutional neural networks.

span.label: the conservation law, taken from physics and imposed on relevance flowing between network layers
span.quote: The underlying Formula (2) can be interpreted as a conservation law for the relevance R in between layers of the feature processing.

span.label: a quantitative test that can separate two heatmaps which look equally good to a human
span.note: eliminates: two heatmapping methods being ranked on how good they look to a human, which is the judgement the paper exists to replace · outcome: partial
span.quote: In this paper we have proposed as a starting point a pixel-flipping method that allows to discriminate between two heatmapping methods that may otherwise look of similar quality to the human.

span.label: a counterexample testing whether the conservation constraint alone yields a meaningful decomposition
span.note: eliminates: the conservation constraint being credited with producing a meaningful decomposition when it constrains only the total · outcome: failed
span.quote: In terms of pixel-wise decomposition interpretation, all inputs point towards the presence of a structure if f(x) > 0 and towards the absence of a structure if f(x) < 0. This is for many classification problems not a realistic interpretation.

span.label: application to a classifier the authors did not train, to show no retraining is needed
span.note: eliminates: a heatmapping result that depends on the authors having trained the classifier themselves · outcome: held
span.quote: This desirable property is demonstrated in this paper by the heatmapping of images classified by the third-party GPU-trained ImageNet neural network. In particular, our heatmapping procedure was applied to this network without any further training or retraining.

span.label: pixel-wise decomposition
span.quote: The overall idea of pixel-wise decomposition is to understand the contribution of a single pixel of an image x to the prediction f(x) made by a classifier f in an image classification task. We would like to find out, separately for each image x, which pixels contribute to what extent to a positive or negative classification result.

span.label: layer-wise relevance propagation
span.quote: We will introduce layer-wise relevance propagation as a concept defined by a set of constraints. Any solution satisfying the constraints will be considered to follow the concept of layer-wise relevance propagation.

span.label: relevance
span.quote: The above example gives furthermore an intuition about what relevance R is, namely, the local contribution to the prediction function f(x). In that sense the relevance of the output layer is the prediction itself f(x).

span.label: heatmap
span.quote: In terms of subsequent visualization, which however will not be the scope of this paper, the resulting relevances R d for each input pixel x (d) can be mapped to a color space and visualized in that way as a conventional heatmap.

span.label: conservation law
span.quote: The underlying Formula (2) can be interpreted as a conservation law for the relevance R in between layers of the feature processing.

span.label: black box
span.quote: However, like many methods in machine learning, these models often lack a straightforward interpretability of the classifier predictions. In other words the classifier acts as a black box and does not provide detailed information about why it reaches a certain classification decision.

span.label: pixel-flipping
span.quote: In this paper we have proposed as a starting point a pixel-flipping method that allows to discriminate between two heatmapping methods that may otherwise look of similar quality to the human.

span.label: segmentation
span.quote: The methods we propose in this paper do not involve segmentation. They do not require pixel-wise training as learning setup or pixel-wise labeling for the training phase. The setup used here is image-wise classification, in which during training one label is provided for an image as a whole, however, the contribution of this paper is not about classifier training. The proposed methods are built on top of a pre-trained classifier.

span.label: pre-trained classifier
span.quote: The methods we propose in this paper do not involve segmentation. They do not require pixel-wise training as learning setup or pixel-wise labeling for the training phase. The setup used here is image-wise classification, in which during training one label is provided for an image as a whole, however, the contribution of this paper is not about classifier training. The proposed methods are built on top of a pre-trained classifier.

span.label: non-linearity
span.quote: This lack of interpretability is due to the non-linearity of the various mappings that process the raw image pixels to its feature representation and from that to the final classifier function.

span.label: Taylor reference point
span.quote: Notably, these two methods were not defined as a particular solution to the heatmapping problem, but instead as a set of constraints that the heatmapping procedure must fulfill in order to be admissible. For instance, the exact choice of Taylor reference point was not specified beyond the constraints that it should be a root and that it should be located close to the actual data point. Similarly, the layer-wise relevance propagation has been defined with the sole restriction that the propagation rule conserves class relevance on a layer and node basis.

span.label: Taylor-type decomposition
span.quote: One alternative approach for achieving a decomposition as in (1) for a general differentiable predictor f is first order Taylor approximation.

span.label: root point
span.quote: Thus, x 0 should be chosen to be a root of the predictor f.

span.label: sensitivity maps
span.quote: Several works have been using sensitivity maps for visualization of classifier predictions which were based on using partial derivatives at the prediction point x.

span.label: Taylor residuum
span.quote: For the sake of precision of the Taylor approximation of the prediction, x 0 should be chosen to be close to x under the Euclidean norm in order to minimize the Taylor residuum according to higher order Taylor approximations.

span.label: locally linear
span.quote: Thus the whole pixel-wise decomposition is not a linear, but a locally linear algorithm, as the root point x 0 depends on the prediction point x.

span.label: layer-wise relevance propagation = whatever satisfies the constraints; several different algorithms qualify
span.quote: It is important to note that the definition is not given as an algorithm or a solution of an objective with a distinct minimum. Instead, it is given as a set of constraints that the solution should satisfy. Thus, different algorithms with different resulting solutions may be admissible under these constraints.

span.label: R_d < 0 = evidence AGAINST the structure being present; R_d > 0 = evidence FOR it
span.quote: The qualitative interpretation is that R d < 0 contributes evidence against the presence of a structure which is to be classified while R d > 0 contributes evidence for its presence.

span.label: relevance at the output layer = the prediction f(x) itself
span.quote: The above example gives furthermore an intuition about what relevance R is, namely, the local contribution to the prediction function f(x). In that sense the relevance of the output layer is the prediction itself f(x).

span.label: heatmap = relevances mapped to a colour space - named, then explicitly put out of scope
span.quote: In terms of subsequent visualization, which however will not be the scope of this paper, the resulting relevances R d for each input pixel x (d) can be mapped to a color space and visualized in that way as a conventional heatmap.

span.label: 'admissible' = satisfying the constraints, which is weaker than 'correct' and the paper says so
span.quote: It is important to note that the definition is not given as an algorithm or a solution of an objective with a distinct minimum. Instead, it is given as a set of constraints that the solution should satisfy. Thus, different algorithms with different resulting solutions may be admissible under these constraints.

span.quote: Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision.

span.label: distinguishes-from → the standard task of optimising a classifier for accuracy and generalisation
span.note: the paper's framing move: explaining one decision is ORTHOGONAL to training a good classifier, so a better classifier does not make a better explanation
span.quote: Making, say, a nonlinear classification decision for one particular novel data point transparent to the user is essentially orthogonal to the standard task of optimizing for an excellent and well generalizing classifier.

span.label: critiques → the claim that non-linear models' success justifies their opacity
span.note: highly successful AND prevented from contributing understanding - the paper puts those in one sentence
span.quote: While highly successful in e.g. hard classification, regression or ranking problems, their non-linearity so far has prevented these models to additionally explain and thus contribute to a better understanding about the nature of the solved problem.

span.label: the two proposed methods are given as constraint sets, so their remaining freedom is deferred to the user
span.quote: Thus, the further specification of relevance propagation rule is deferred to the appreciation of the user, or as a future work, and may either be model-specific, problem-specific, or subject to a particular practical or computational requirement.

span.label: there is no direct relationship between a classifier's value at a point and its derivative at the same point, which is the first reason a gradient map is not an explanation
span.quote: Firstly, there is no direct relationship between the function value f(x) at the prediction point x and the differential Df(x) at the same point x.

span.label: derivatives at the prediction point are stated to be UNSUITABLE for the paper's aim - a rejection of the dominant visualisation method of the time
span.quote: Therefore derivatives at the prediction point x are not useful for achieving our aim.

span.label: layer-wise relevance propagation needs no second reference point at all, which is the practical advantage claimed over Taylor decomposition
span.quote: Unlike the Taylor approximation, layer-wise relevance propagation does not require to use a second point besides the input point.

span.quote: In this example the explanation vector from the local gradient at the prediction point x has a too large contribution in an irrelevant direction.
